content:
Over the past couple of days, two separate reports have indicated that Apple is working in two different directions with the goal of boosting overall profitability by increasing services revenue.

In my view, Apple should absolutely be doing the former, but not the latter — and it looks like Phil Schiller would seem to agree…

First, a quick summary of the two reports.

Home security and monitoring service

Bloomberg reported on Friday that Apple is planning to launch an all-new home security and monitoring service, to be introduced alongside the new home hardware we've been expecting.

Squeezing more revenue from the App Store

The same source published a second report on Sunday, saying Apple is exploring various ways to extract more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple shouldn't do the latter

Taking them in reverse order, I believe the second approach would be a huge mistake.

Apple's effective monopoly position over iPhone app sales is already being challenged by regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you have to do it via the official App Store, leaving you with no choice but to accept Apple's take-it-or-leave-it terms.

I understand the general argument that nobody is forced to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but even the most laissez-faire form of capitalism doesn't actually work that way in practice: the US has had antitrust laws since 1890 for precisely this reason. Once your market dominance reaches a certain point, you become subject to various constraints to ensure you don't abuse your position.

Trying to squeeze more money out of the App Store is the very opposite of "skating to where the puck is going." Phil Schiller is reportedly of the same view, and Bloomberg cited this as one of the reasons for his current gradual step-back.

Innovative services are the right direction

By contrast, launching genuinely innovative services that people want to buy is the right direction for Apple to take. I can absolutely see the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

I argued back in 2024 that making its own smart home cameras would be … one of the smartest moves Apple could make. I feel the same way about the rumored Apple smart doorbell. For security products, offering an optional service bundle has two very compelling reasons behind it.

First, there are all the privacy reasons I've outlined before. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal to safeguard the privacy of security camera footage. If I had to pick a company to handle AI analysis of security camera footage, I'd pick Apple.

Second, Apple is of course uniquely positioned to fully integrate security hardware and services into the HomeKit environment. I'm sure there are many other areas in which Apple could offer similar benefits.

For me, the key thing is that Apple needs to treat services with the same approach as hardware: make excellent products, and let people willingly — even happily — pay for them. Not extract money in ways that leave customers, developers, and regulators all feeling resentful.

What are your views on this? Please share them in the comments.
